title: LLM quick hits and experiment scratchpad (March 2026)
content:
Purpose: quick, messy brain dump of papers/blogs and small experiments I want to try on inference cost/latency tradeoffs. Not polished — notes to self.

Context and motivation:
- Trying to get a feel for low-cost LLM serving for medium-tail workloads (conversational agents with ~5k active users, lots of short interactions).
- Focus areas: KV caching strategies, tiny model variants for fallback, low-bit quantization PTQ with minimal latency overhead, and routing ideas for small-scale MoE-like capacity.
- Keep pragmatic: target is end-to-end 99th pctl latency < 200ms for 90% of requests, token-cost down 2x vs baseline.

Quick takeaways from recent reads:
- FlashAttention and kernel-level improvements still matter: memory access patterns dominate on short sequences. For 1-2 token step generation, micro-optimizations (fused softmax, blocked GEMMs) reduce kernel launch overheads. If we can reduce launch count via continuous-batching, wins compound.
- KV-MoE style sharding (sparse experts only on KV so compute routing cheap) is interesting — can act as a lightweight capacity expansion without full MLP routing. But routing staleness and memory blowup are real concerns.
- Quantization: AWQ-style PTQ (per-channel scale + outlier handling) seems to retain quality for many LLMs at 4-bit with relatively simple calibration. However, latency regressions due to dequant/req conversions can erase theoretical speedups. Need quant kernels integrated into runtime.
- Caching: prefix/KV caching yields big cost win for repeated prompts. Two notes: 1) Cache key strategy — include user persona + prompt template hash to avoid pollution. 2) TTL policy should be workload-aware (high-turnover chat vs static retrieval-heavy flows).

Papers / blog quick hits to re-check:
- FlashAttention (Tay et al.) — re-skim for small-seq perf graphs and kernel notes.
- AWQ / SmoothQuant implementations — compare calibration sample sizes for PTQ.
- KV-MoE blog + ICLR talk (Jordan/others) — routing impl details and memory accounting.
- HuggingFace thread: FP16 vs 4-bit inference perf on Ampere vs Blackwell.

Open questions / hypotheses:
1) Continuous batching + tiny-batch GPU kernels: can we get real wall-clock latency improvements for 1-4 token steps vs naive single-token generation? Hypothesis: yes if kernel count reduced and KV copying minimized.
2) 4-bit PTQ + fused dequant in-kernel: should beat FP16 on cost per token once we eliminate roundtrip conversions. Need to measure both throughput and p99 latency.
3) KV-MoE as a fallback tier: route heavy-context requests to a shard with expanded KV memory (cheaper than full MoE). Risk: routing complexity and tail latencies.

Experiment ideas (small, runnable) — prioritize low-effort, high-info:
- A: Microbench: baseline generate step for Llama2-13B FP16 vs 4-bit AWQ on p4 vs h100-80. Metrics: median step latency (1 token), p95/p99, kernel timelines. Use same batch sizes: 1, 4, 8 concurrent streams.
- B: Continuous batching simulation: synthetic stream of short chats (turn length 3 tokens avg). Implement a small event loop that groups inflight requests to a single worker up to 8ms window. Measure latency distribution and throughput vs no-batch.
- C: KV TTL experiment: synthetic prompt set with 20% repeated prefixes. Vary cache TTLs 1s/10s/60s and measure token compute saved vs cache overhead.
- D: Simple KV-sparse-expert prototype: keep base model frozen, add small per-user KV memory (128-dim) stored in an expert table. At inference, concatenate XOR of top-k memories into KV and route only when similarity > threshold. Measure memory footprint and latency.

Practical notes for infra (runtime constraints):
- Any quant experiment needs a path to integrate custom kernels into our serving runtime (traceable PR path). If that is high friction, measure perf on standalone bench and hand off to infra with perf profile.
- SRE concern: caching increases memory pressure unpredictable spikes — need eviction heuristics measured under adversarial users.
- For continuous-batching, need backpressure tuning so interactive clients don't see huge jitter. Worth a guardrail: max batching delay 10ms.

Snippets / commands to re-run later:
- baseline bench (local): python bench_step.py --model llama-13b-fp16 --device cuda:0 --batch 1 --seq 1
- awq quant: python quantize_awq.py --model path/to/checkpoint --calib 1024 --out 4bit-awq
- continuous batch sim: python simulate_streams.py --arrival-poisson --lambda 20/s --window-ms 8

Quality checks to include in evals:
- Per-sample perplexity + end-task metric (RAG quality or dialog BLEU/ROUGE where applicable) after quant/PTQ. Small deltas in PPL can hide big task drop for some prompts — keep a small human eval set.
- Generation stability tests: targeted prompts that previously caused degenerate repeats or truncation in low-bit conversions.

To-dos (short list):
- [ ] Run microbench A on H100-80 (ask infra for 2h allocation). DM Daniel to share his bench scripts.
- [ ] Prototype continuous-batching sim (2-3 hours). Aim to get latency distribution plot.
- [ ] Draft short note for infra about embedding fused dequant kernel feasibility (one pager).
- [ ] Collect 50 prompts that represent our product's heavy tails (edge cases).

Random ideas for later (parking lot):
- Hybrid fallback where a tiny distilled model handles greeting/closing utterances and main model invoked for long-tail semantics.
- Dynamic precision: start generation in 4-bit, switch to FP16 when model enters uncertain state (high entropy) — but switching cost might be high.

Notes to self: keep this very iterative. Focus experiments that reduce unit cost without breaking 95/99 latency SLO. If something looks promising, package a short reproducible benchmark and hand to infra.

End.
